subject: mathematics
question_text: Use mathematical induction to prove that 2 + 3·2 + 4·2² + … up to n terms = n·2ⁿ, ∀ n ∈ N.

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), book p.30, chapter 4 MATHEMATICAL INDUCTION, Short Answer question 9. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The split gives one mark to each of the four moves an induction proof is marked on — the base case, the hypothesis, the inductive step and the closing appeal to the principle — and leaves the opening statement step unmarked, matching every other card in this chapter. The nth term is read off the printed pattern as (n+1)·2ⁿ⁻¹, which reproduces 2, 3·2, 4·2² at n = 1, 2, 3 and gives the stated sum n·2ⁿ at n = 1, 2 and 3; that reading is ours, since the book states only the first three terms. Paper position: Maths-1A Section B prints eight short answers of which the student writes any six, each worth 4 marks, and Mathematical Induction supplies one of them on almost every paper. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this by induction — how you read the nth term off the pattern, and how the powers of 2 combine in the third step.

steps.label: Find the nth term
steps.margin_note: Unmarked setup at 4 marks, and the step most students get wrong. Two things change from term to term: the number in front goes 2, 3, 4 and the power of 2 goes 0, 1, 2.

recall.must_convey: That the nth term is (n+1)·2ⁿ⁻¹ — the coefficient is n + 1 and the power of 2 is n − 1 — and that S(n) is the full statement.
accept: the nth term is n plus one times two to the n minus one
the number in front goes two three four so it is n plus one and the power goes zero one two so it is n minus one
general term n plus one into two power n minus one then write out s of n
nth term n plus one into two power n minus one ani rastam
heard_as: two to the n minus one

steps.why: The first term is written as 2, which hides the fact that it is 2·2⁰. Writing all three given terms with their powers of 2 shown is what makes the pattern readable.
common_mistakes: Reading the nth term as n·2ⁿ⁻¹, which gives 1, 2·2, 3·2² and not the printed series.
Reading the power of 2 as n instead of n − 1, so the first term comes out as 4.
steps.memory_tip: Write the first term as 2·2⁰. Then the front numbers are n + 1 and the powers are n − 1.

steps.label: Check S(1)
steps.margin_note: One mark. Work out BOTH sides separately at n = 1 and say they are equal.
lines: ∴ L.H.S = R.H.S, so S(1) is true.

recall.must_convey: That at n = 1 the left side is 2 times 2 to the power 0, which is 2, and the right side is 1 times 2, which is also 2.
accept: left side is two times two to the zero which is two and right side is one times two which is two
put n equals one in both sides and both come to two
the first case gives two on each side
n equals one pettina rendu sides two vasthai

steps.why: Using the nth term formula at n = 1 rather than just copying the printed 2 is what checks that (n+1)·2ⁿ⁻¹ was read correctly. At n = 2 both sides give 8, which is a second check worth doing in rough work.
common_mistakes: Asserting S(1) is true without working out both sides.
steps.memory_tip: At n = 1: left side 2·2⁰ = 2, right side 1·2¹ = 2. At n = 2 both sides give 8.

steps.label: Assume S(k) is true
steps.margin_note: One mark. Assume it for ONE value k and number the line (1) — Step 3 quotes that number.
lines: Step 2 — assume S(k) is true, k ∈ N

recall.must_convey: That S(k) is assumed true for some k in N — the sum of k terms equals k times 2 to the k — and the line is numbered (1).
accept: assume the sum of k terms is k times two to the k
suppose s of k holds and call that equation one
take it as true for one value k in the naturals and number the line
k ki true ani assume chesi equation one ga rastam
reject: let it be true for k
then I assume s of k
heard_as: k times two to the k

steps.why: This is the assumption the method rests on. It is granted for one value only, and Step 3 has to earn the right to pass it on to the next value.
common_mistakes: Assuming the statement for ALL k, which assumes what is being proved.
Writing the last term as (k+1)·2ᵏ instead of (k+1)·2ᵏ⁻¹.
steps.memory_tip: Replace n by k everywhere, including inside the power. Number the line (1).

steps.label: Show S(k+1) follows
steps.margin_note: One mark, and the longest step on the page. The next term is (k+2)·2ᵏ. Both terms carry 2ᵏ, so take it out and the rest is easy.
lines: Add it to both sides of (1):
So S(k+1) is true whenever S(k) is true.

recall.must_convey: That the next term is (k+2)·2ᵏ, both terms share 2ᵏ, and 2k + 2 is 2(k+1), so the 2 joins the power to give (k+1)·2ᵏ⁺¹.
accept: the next term is k plus two into two to the k so take two to the k out and you get two k plus two
two k plus two is two into k plus one and that two raises the power to k plus one
add the next term and it becomes k plus one times two to the k plus one
next term add chesi two power k common teeste k plus one vasthundi
reject: I show s of k plus one
heard_as: two to the k plus one

steps.why: Both terms already carry 2ᵏ, so the whole step is one factorisation. The spare 2 inside 2(k+1) is what pushes the power from 2ᵏ up to 2ᵏ⁺¹.
common_mistakes: Writing the next term as (k+1)·2ᵏ — put n = k+1 into (n+1)·2ⁿ⁻¹ and the coefficient is k + 2.
Leaving the answer as 2ᵏ(2k+2) and not turning the spare 2 into the higher power.
Stopping before writing = R.H.S, so the step does not show what was asked.
steps.memory_tip: Take 2ᵏ out: k + (k+2) = 2k + 2 = 2(k+1), and that spare 2 lifts 2ᵏ to 2ᵏ⁺¹.

steps.label: Conclude by P.M.I
steps.margin_note: The last mark is for naming the principle. One sentence, one full mark.
lines: Hence, by the principle of finite

recall.must_convey: That S(1) is true and S(k) implies S(k+1), so by the principle of mathematical induction the result holds for every natural number n.
accept: since s of one is true and s of k gives s of k plus one by the principle of mathematical induction it holds for all n
hence by p m i the statement is true for every natural number
the base case and the inductive step together give it for all n in n
p m i prakaram anni natural numbers ki true

steps.why: The earlier steps prove two single statements — one about n = 1 and one about a step. Only the principle turns them into a claim about every n.
common_mistakes: Writing only 'hence proved' and never naming the principle.
Claiming it for all real numbers instead of all n ∈ N.
steps.memory_tip: The closing sentence names the principle and is worth a full mark on its own.
